title: Indian American Rep. Shri Thanedar Loses Michigan Primary to Progressive Challenger
excerpt: DSA-backed state lawmaker Donavan McKinney defeats the two-term incumbent 52-48 in a race that tested progressive momentum in a majority-Black district.
body:
• Rep. Shri Thanedar (D-MI), one of the most prominent Indian-born members of Congress, lost his Democratic primary to state Rep. Donavan McKinney by a margin of 52% to 48%.
  • McKinney was backed by Bernie Sanders, Rashida Tlaib, and the Democratic Socialists of America; Thanedar had the support of House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and pro-Israel group AIPAC.
  • Thanedar first won the seat in 2022 with just 28% of the vote in a crowded primary; this year McKinney was the sole Black challenger, consolidating the district's majority-Black vote.
  • Michigan's 13th Congressional District is safely Democratic, making McKinney the prohibitive favourite for November's general election.

Rep. Shri Thanedar, the Indian-born Democratic congressman representing Michigan's 13th Congressional District, lost his primary on Tuesday to state Rep. Donavan McKinney by a margin of 52% to 48%, according to the Associated Press and NBC News.

The defeat ends Thanedar's two-term run in Congress and removes one of the highest-profile Indian American voices from the U.S. House. McKinney, backed by the Democratic Socialists of America and a coalition of progressive endorsers, will face Republican T.P. Nykoriak in November in a district that voted for Kamala Harris by 41 points in 2024.

From Poverty in India to Congress

Thanedar's political story was itself a remarkable immigrant narrative. Born Shrinivas Prasad Thanedar in Chikkodi, in what is now Karnataka, he grew up in poverty — his family home sometimes lacked running water and electricity. He arrived in the United States in 1979 with a chemistry degree and $20, earned a PhD from the University of Akron, and built pharmaceutical research companies that employed hundreds of people. Ernst & Young named him Entrepreneur of the Year three times.

He entered politics through the Michigan state legislature in 2020, then won the 13th District's Democratic primary in 2022 with 28% of the vote in a nine-candidate field. His victory was controversial: he was the only non-Black candidate in a majority-Black district, and multiple Black candidates split the Black vote. When he was sworn in, Detroit lost Black congressional representation for the first time since 1955.

A Consolidation Race

This year's primary was structurally different. McKinney was the only Black candidate challenging Thanedar, consolidating support that had been fragmented across multiple challengers in previous cycles.

McKinney secured endorsements from Sen. Bernie Sanders, Rep. Rashida Tlaib, Rep. Ilhan Omar, Rep. Ayanna Pressley, and Justice Democrats. The Metro Detroit DSA chapter organised aggressively for him, with volunteers travelling from New York to canvass Detroit neighbourhoods.

"Today, we showed why being always with the people is more than a slogan — it's a road map for the Democratic Party on how to move forward to defeat the fascism and divisiveness harming our country, and to deliver the leadership the Mighty 13th deserves."

— Donavan McKinney, in his victory statement

Thanedar countered with the backing of House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and AIPAC, emphasising his efforts to fight the Trump administration and his impeachment resolution against the president. He funded his campaigns heavily from personal wealth — over $13.6 million across three congressional runs, according to campaign finance filings.

Policy Fault Lines

While both candidates supported Medicare for All, they diverged sharply on foreign policy. Thanedar was aligned with pro-Israel groups, while McKinney called for an end to U.S. military support for Israel — a position with growing traction in the heavily progressive district.

Thanedar had briefly affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America before leaving the organisation in 2023 over what he called its failure to condemn Hamas's October 7 attack. McKinney's DSA endorsement made the race a national test of whether the organisation could expand its support base beyond its traditional constituency of college-educated white progressives.

What It Means for Indian American Representation

Thanedar's loss thins the ranks of Indian-born members in Congress at a time when Indian Americans are one of the fastest-growing political demographics in the country. He was the first Indian American to represent Michigan in Congress, and his rags-to-riches biography gave him a unique profile within the Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus.

The defeat also underscores the limits of self-funded campaigns in an era of heightened grassroots organising. McKinney's campaign criticised Thanedar for having "bought his seat," pointing to the role of personal wealth and crypto-linked PAC spending in his previous victories.

What's Next

Michigan's 13th District — which encompasses much of Detroit, Hamtramck, Highland Park, the Grosse Pointes, and several Downriver communities — will almost certainly send McKinney to Congress in January 2027. His victory was part of a broader progressive sweep in Michigan's August primaries, which also saw Abdul El-Sayed win the Democratic U.S. Senate nomination and climate activist William Lawrence capture a battleground House seat.
nri_angle: Thanedar's defeat ends the tenure of one of the most prominent Indian-born members of Congress, raising questions about Indian American political representation in the Midwest.
